title: Loading & Error UI (loading.tsx, error.tsx, not-found)
summary: The App Router gives each route segment its own **loading.tsx**, **error.tsx**, and **not-found.tsx** files that Next.js wires up automatically — `loading.tsx` shows an instant fallback via React **Suspense**, `error.tsx` is a per-segment error boundary with a `reset()` retry, and `notFound()` renders the nearest `not-found.tsx`.

subtopics.title: loading.tsx (instant loading states)
subtopics.explanation: A `loading.tsx` in a route segment is automatically wrapped around that segment's `page.tsx` in a React `<Suspense>` boundary. While the async Server Component awaits data, Next streams the loading fallback to the browser instantly, then swaps in the real content when it's ready — no manual Suspense wiring needed.

subtopics.title: error.tsx (per-segment error boundary)
subtopics.explanation: An `error.tsx` is a Client Component (it must start with `'use client'`) that Next.js turns into an Error Boundary around the segment. If rendering the segment throws, Next renders `error.tsx` instead of crashing the whole app. It receives an `error` prop and a `reset()` function.

subtopics.title: reset() — recovering from errors
subtopics.explanation: The `reset()` function passed to `error.tsx` re-attempts to render the segment's contents without a full page reload. It's the recovery path: a transient failure (a flaky fetch) can be retried in place, keeping the surrounding layout and navigation intact.

subtopics.title: not-found.tsx + notFound()
subtopics.explanation: Calling the `notFound()` helper from a Server Component throws a special error that Next catches and renders the nearest `not-found.tsx` with a 404 status. It's the idiomatic way to say 'this resource doesn't exist' — e.g. an unknown product slug.
subtopics.example:
import { notFound } from 'next/navigation';
if (!product) notFound(); // renders not-found.tsx, status 404

subtopics.title: global-error.tsx (root boundary)
subtopics.explanation: A segment-level `error.tsx` cannot catch errors thrown in the root layout itself, because it lives inside that layout. `global-error.tsx` is the last-resort boundary that wraps the entire app — it must render its own `<html>` and `<body>` because the broken layout is replaced.

subtopics.title: Nested boundaries (segment isolation)
subtopics.explanation: Because each segment can have its own loading/error files, failures and loading states are isolated to that part of the tree. A nested `error.tsx` catches errors below it while the parent layout stays interactive — so one broken widget never takes down the whole page.
subtopics.example:
app/
  layout.tsx       // survives
  feed/error.tsx   // catches feed errors only

foundations.overview: In the App Router, loading and error UI are file conventions, not boilerplate you write by hand. Dropping a `loading.tsx`, `error.tsx`, or `not-found.tsx` into a route segment tells Next.js to automatically wrap that segment in a Suspense boundary and an Error Boundary, giving you instant loading fallbacks and graceful failure handling scoped to exactly that part of the UI.
foundations.formalDefinition: `loading.tsx` defines a Suspense fallback for a segment; `error.tsx` defines a React Error Boundary (a Client Component receiving `error` and `reset`) for a segment; `not-found.tsx` defines the UI rendered when `notFound()` is called or a route is unmatched; `global-error.tsx` is the root-level error boundary wrapping the whole app.
foundations.whyItMatters: These conventions turn two notoriously fiddly UX concerns — showing something while data loads and recovering gracefully when it fails — into single files. They give users immediate feedback and keep the rest of the app alive when one segment breaks, which is the difference between a polished app and a white screen of death.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture each route segment wrapped in two invisible boxes: an outer Error Boundary (`error.tsx`) and an inner Suspense boundary (`loading.tsx`). Async work suspends → the loading box shows its fallback. A throw → the error box shows its fallback with a retry. `notFound()` is a special throw that the framework routes to `not-found.tsx`.
foundations.browserPerspective: With `loading.tsx`, the browser receives the layout plus the loading fallback as the first streamed HTML chunk, paints it immediately, then receives and swaps in the real content when the server finishes — so the user never stares at a blank screen during navigation.
foundations.realWorldUsage: A dashboard shows a skeleton via `loading.tsx` while charts fetch; a product page calls `notFound()` for unknown slugs to render a 404; a checkout step uses `error.tsx` with `reset()` so a failed payment lookup can be retried without losing the page.
foundations.businessImpact: Instant loading states reduce perceived latency and bounce rates, while scoped error recovery keeps users in the funnel instead of bouncing on a crash — both directly affect conversion and retention.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Standardizing on file conventions removes hand-rolled Suspense/ErrorBoundary plumbing and inconsistent loaders across a codebase, making error/loading behavior predictable and reviewable per route.
foundations.performanceImpact: Because loading.tsx streams a fallback as the first chunk, time-to-first-byte feels instant and the page becomes interactive progressively, rather than waiting for all data before sending any HTML.
commonUseCases: Skeleton/spinner UI while a segment fetches data (loading.tsx)
Per-segment recovery from transient fetch/render failures (error.tsx + reset)
404 pages for missing resources via notFound() + not-found.tsx
App-wide fallback when the root layout itself throws (global-error.tsx)

commonMisconceptions.myth: error.tsx can be a Server Component.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It must be a Client Component ('use client') because it needs state, an Error Boundary, and the interactive reset() handler.

commonMisconceptions.myth: error.tsx catches every error in the app, including the root layout.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A segment's error.tsx lives inside its parent layout, so it cannot catch errors thrown by that layout or the root layout — global-error.tsx handles those.

steps.name: Navigate
steps.detail: User navigates to /dashboard. Next renders the layout immediately and suspends the async page while it awaits data.

steps.name: loading.tsx
steps.detail: The Suspense fallback from loading.tsx streams to the browser first, so the user sees a skeleton instantly instead of a blank screen.

steps.name: Resolve
steps.detail: When the data resolves, the real page content streams in and replaces the fallback in place — the layout never re-rendered.

steps.name: error.tsx
steps.detail: If the segment throws while rendering, the Error Boundary from error.tsx renders instead, showing a message and a Try again button.

steps.name: reset()
steps.detail: Clicking Try again calls reset(), which re-attempts rendering the segment without a full reload, recovering from transient failures.

steps.name: notFound()
steps.detail: If the page calls notFound(), Next renders the nearest not-found.tsx with a 404 status instead of an error.

codeLab.title: Build a loading-then-error flow with retry
codeLab.instructions: Implement a component that shows a loading state, then either content or an error with a working retry. Fill in the loading UI and the reset handler so the broken state can recover. Then Run.
codeLab.expectedOutput: Loading state, then an error with a Try again button that recovers to 'Loaded!'.
hints: The loading branch is your loading.tsx fallback — render a skeleton or spinner.
reset() should move the state out of 'error' so the segment re-renders successfully.

debuggingLab.title: Why doesn't my error.tsx catch the error?
debuggingLab.symptom: An error thrown while rendering a route crashes the app instead of showing the nice error.tsx UI, and the console warns about Client Component hooks in a Server Component.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: error.tsx must be a Client Component because Error Boundaries rely on React class/state internals and the reset() handler needs to run in the browser. Without 'use client' at the top of the file, Next can't register it as the segment's Error Boundary, so the error propagates up and crashes the app.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the 'use client' directive at the top of error.tsx.
Expecting a segment's error.tsx to catch errors thrown by its parent or root layout (use global-error.tsx for that).
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Mark the error file as a Client Component and wire up a working reset() that re-renders the segment.

theory.question: What do loading.tsx and error.tsx do in the App Router, and how does Next wire them up?
theory.directAnswer: `loading.tsx` defines a fallback that Next automatically wraps around the segment's page in a React Suspense boundary, so the fallback streams instantly while the async page awaits data. `error.tsx` is a Client Component that Next turns into an Error Boundary around the segment; if rendering throws, it renders instead and receives `error` and `reset` props so the user can retry. Both are file conventions scoped to their route segment.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two automatic boundaries per segment: a Suspense boundary (loading.tsx) and an Error Boundary (error.tsx).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To make loading states and error recovery declarative file conventions instead of hand-written Suspense/ErrorBoundary wrappers in every route.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Next wraps page.tsx in <Suspense fallback={<Loading/>}> when loading.tsx exists, and in an Error Boundary that renders error.tsx (a 'use client' component) when it exists.

theory.whyImportant: These conventions are core App Router knowledge and show whether a candidate understands Suspense, streaming, and segment-scoped UI.
theory.realWorldExample: A dashboard route streams a skeleton from loading.tsx, then swaps in charts; if a chart's fetch throws, error.tsx shows a retry button via reset().

nestedTopics.title: Suspense wiring
nestedTopics.explanation: loading.tsx is sugar for wrapping the page in <Suspense fallback>.

nestedTopics.title: Client requirement
nestedTopics.explanation: error.tsx must be 'use client' because Error Boundaries and reset need browser interactivity.

followUps.question: Why must error.tsx be a Client Component?
followUps.answer: Because Error Boundaries depend on React internals/state and reset() must run interactively in the browser.

followUps.question: Where does the loading fallback show during navigation?
followUps.answer: It streams as the first HTML chunk after the layout, so the user sees it immediately while the page's data resolves.

theory.question: What's the difference between error.tsx, not-found.tsx, and global-error.tsx?
theory.directAnswer: `error.tsx` catches unexpected errors thrown while rendering a segment and offers a reset() retry. `not-found.tsx` renders intentional 404 UI when `notFound()` is called or a route is unmatched. `global-error.tsx` is the root-level Error Boundary that catches errors in the root layout itself — which a segment's error.tsx can't — and must render its own <html> and <body> because the broken layout is replaced.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Three distinct fallbacks: segment error, intentional 404, and app-wide root error.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Errors, missing resources, and root-layout failures are different cases that deserve different UI and HTTP semantics.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: notFound() throws a special error caught by the framework to render not-found.tsx (404); other throws bubble to the nearest error.tsx, then to global-error.tsx if they reach the root.

theory.whyImportant: Distinguishing intentional 404s from unexpected errors and knowing where the root boundary lives is a frequent App Router discriminator.
theory.realWorldExample: Unknown product slug -> notFound() -> not-found.tsx (404); a broken root layout -> global-error.tsx full-page fallback.

nestedTopics.title: HTTP status
nestedTopics.explanation: not-found.tsx responds with 404; error boundaries respond with 500-class errors.

nestedTopics.title: Root boundary scope
nestedTopics.explanation: global-error.tsx replaces the entire app shell, so it owns its own html/body tags.

followUps.question: Why can't a segment error.tsx catch root layout errors?
followUps.answer: It renders inside its parent/root layout, so a failure in that layout happens above the boundary; global-error.tsx wraps everything.

scenario.question: One widget on a dashboard occasionally throws and takes down the whole page. How do you isolate it?
scenario.directAnswer: I'd move that widget into its own route segment (or its own Suspense/Error boundary) and add an `error.tsx` scoped to it. Because error boundaries are per-segment, the failure is contained to that widget — it shows a retry via reset() while the surrounding layout and other widgets stay interactive. I'd also add a loading.tsx so its slow fetch doesn't block the rest of the page.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A boundary-scoping problem: an unscoped failure crashes the whole tree.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Without a nearby error boundary, the error bubbles up to a higher boundary that wraps everything.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Placing error.tsx/loading.tsx at the widget's segment confines both failures and loading to that subtree.

scenario.whyImportant: Segment isolation is the key resilience pattern in the App Router.

nestedTopics.title: Granular boundaries
nestedTopics.explanation: Smaller segments mean smaller blast radius for both loading and errors.

nestedTopics.title: Streaming
nestedTopics.explanation: Independent loading.tsx fallbacks let parts of the page stream in separately.

followUps.question: How would you also log the error?
followUps.answer: Use the useEffect in error.tsx to report error/error.digest to your monitoring service when the boundary renders.

coding.question: Write a route segment's loading.tsx, error.tsx, and a page that calls notFound() for missing data.
coding.thoughtProcess: loading.tsx is a simple server component returning a fallback. error.tsx must be a Client Component with 'use client', receiving { error, reset }. The page is an async Server Component that fetches and calls notFound() when the resource is missing.
coding.lineByLine: loading.tsx returns the Suspense fallback Next streams while the page awaits getProduct. error.tsx starts with 'use client', logs the error in an effect, and calls reset() to retry. The page awaits the data and, when it's missing, calls notFound() which throws to render the nearest not-found.tsx with a 404 status.
coding.timeComplexity: N/A — UI conventions, not an algorithm.

alternativeApproaches.title: Inline Suspense
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Wrap a slow child in <Suspense> inside the page for finer-grained streaming instead of a segment-wide loading.tsx.

followUps.question: What status code does notFound() produce?
followUps.answer: It renders not-found.tsx and responds with HTTP 404.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Place loading.tsx and error.tsx at the granularity that matches your failure/latency domains: a segment per independently-loading region. Use notFound() for missing resources, dedicated not-found.tsx for friendly 404s, and a single global-error.tsx as the app-wide safety net that renders its own html/body.
productionDeepDive.performance: loading.tsx enables streaming: the layout and fallback paint immediately while data resolves, improving perceived performance. Keep fallbacks lightweight (skeletons) so the first chunk is tiny, and scope boundaries so slow regions don't block fast ones.
productionDeepDive.security: Never render raw error details to users in production error.tsx UI; show a generic message and log the real error (and error.digest) server-side. notFound() avoids leaking whether a resource exists vs. is forbidden when paired with proper authorization.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Segment-scoped boundaries keep the blast radius of a failing dependency small, so one degraded service only fails its widget. This isolation is what lets large apps stay partially available under partial outages.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: File conventions make loading/error behavior consistent and discoverable across the codebase — reviewers find them by path, not by hunting for hand-rolled boundaries. Co-locate them with the segment they protect.
productionDeepDive.observability: Use the useEffect in error.tsx to report errors (with error.digest) to Sentry/your APM. Track 404 rates from not-found.tsx and the frequency of reset() retries to find flaky dependencies.

caseStudies.problem: A single flaky third-party widget intermittently crashed entire pages.
caseStudies.solution: Wrapped each risky region in its own segment with error.tsx + reset() and loading.tsx, isolating failures.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: More files/boundaries to maintain vs. dramatically smaller failure blast radius.
caseStudies.lessons: Granular boundaries keep pages partially available; never let one widget take down the whole route.

keyTakeaways: loading.tsx auto-wraps a segment in Suspense, streaming an instant fallback while the async page loads.
error.tsx is a 'use client' Error Boundary per segment that receives error and a reset() retry function.
notFound() throws a special error that renders the nearest not-found.tsx with an HTTP 404.
global-error.tsx is the root safety net for root-layout failures and must render its own html/body.
Boundaries are per-segment, so loading states and errors stay isolated — one broken widget won't crash the whole page.
